3.3.1:
Why this matters

"The new dispatch method is faster." "Night shift makes more errors." "The new supplier's pallets are stronger." Hypothesis testing is how Six Sigma checks claims like these with data instead of opinion. It is the central tool of the Analyze phase: it is how suspected X's become validated root causes.

The big idea

Every sample varies by chance. If night shift's error rate this week was 4.1% and day shift's was 3.6%, is night shift really worse, or is that difference just random noise? A hypothesis test answers: "If there were truly no difference, how surprising would data like ours be?" If the answer is "very surprising", we conclude there is a real difference.

It works like a court trial:

  • The defendant is presumed innocent (no difference) until proven guilty.
  • The evidence must be strong enough to convict "beyond reasonable doubt".
  • A "not guilty" verdict does not prove innocence; it means the evidence was not strong enough.

The two hypotheses

  • Null hypothesis (H₀): the "nothing is going on" statement: no difference, no effect, the status quo, equality. "Mean load time = 40 minutes." "Day and night error rates are equal." H₀ always contains an equals sign.
  • Alternative hypothesis (Hₐ or H₁): what you are looking for evidence of: a difference (≠), or a difference in a specific direction (< or >). "Mean load time ≠ 40." "Night error rate > day error rate."

The steps

  1. Practical problem: what business question are we answering?
  2. State H₀ and Hₐ.
  3. Choose α (the significance level, usually 0.05): how much risk of a false alarm you accept.
  4. Choose the test (3.3.4) based on data type, number of groups and so on.
  5. Determine the sample size needed (3.2.2), considering power.
  6. Collect the data (randomly, following the data collection plan).
  7. Compute the test statistic and p-value (usually with software).
  8. Decide: compare the p-value with α.
  9. State the practical conclusion in business language.

The p-value

The p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as yours, if H₀ were true.

  • A small p-value means your data would be very unusual if there were no real difference, so you have evidence against H₀.
  • A large p-value means your data are quite consistent with H₀.

Decision rule:

  • p ≤ α → reject H₀. There is statistically significant evidence for Hₐ.
  • p > α → fail to reject H₀. There is not enough evidence for Hₐ.

Memory aid: "If p is low, the null must go. If p is high, the null will fly."

Never "accept" H₀

Failing to reject H₀ does not prove it is true. It means the evidence was not strong enough, perhaps because the sample was too small to detect a real difference. Say "fail to reject H₀" or "no significant evidence of a difference", never "accept H₀" or "proved there is no difference".

One-tailed vs two-tailed

  • Two-tailed test: Hₐ is "≠" (different in either direction). The α risk is split between both tails (2.5% in each for α = 0.05).
  • One-tailed test: Hₐ is "<" or ">" (different in one specific direction). All of α sits in one tail.

A two-tailed test at α = 0.05: results beyond ±1.96 (for a z test) lead to rejecting H₀.

Use a one-tailed test only when a difference in the other direction is genuinely irrelevant and was decided before seeing the data.

Independent vs paired samples

  • Independent samples: two separate groups of units (loads from Terminal A versus loads from Terminal B).
  • Paired samples: two measurements on the same units (each driver's fuel economy before and after training). Pairing removes unit-to-unit differences and makes the test more sensitive (3.4.1).

Confidence intervals and tests agree

A two-sided test at α = 0.05 and a 95% confidence interval give the same decision: if the 95% interval for a difference excludes the hypothesized value (often zero), reject H₀; if it includes it, fail to reject.

Worked example

A carrier wants to know whether average unload time differs from the 40-minute standard. A sample of 25 unloads gives a p-value of 0.08 (α = 0.05).

  • H₀: μ = 40. Hₐ: μ ≠ 40.
  • p = 0.08 > 0.05 → fail to reject H₀.
  • Conclusion: there is not enough evidence that the average unload time differs from 40 minutes. (Not: "the average is 40 minutes.")

If p had been 0.02, the conclusion would be: reject H₀; the average unload time differs significantly from 40 minutes.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • p = 0.08 with α = 0.05 → fail to reject.
  • Never say "accept H₀".
  • H₀ contains the equals sign; Hₐ contains ≠, < or >.
  • The p-value is not the probability that H₀ is true. It is the probability of data this extreme if H₀ were true.

Check yourself

  1. Write H₀ and Hₐ for: "Is the new route faster than the old average of 6.2 hours?"
  2. p = 0.03, α = 0.05. Decision?
  3. p = 0.30. What can you conclude, and what can you not?
  4. A 95% CI for the difference in means is 1.2 to 3.8. Is the difference significant at α = 0.05?
  5. Each driver's fuel economy is measured before and after training. Independent or paired?
Show answers
  1. H₀: μ = 6.2 (or μ ≥ 6.2). Hₐ: μ < 6.2 (one-tailed).
  2. Reject H₀ (p ≤ α).
  3. Fail to reject H₀: no significant evidence of a difference. You cannot conclude there is no difference.
  4. Yes: the interval excludes zero.
  5. Paired.

Key takeaways

  • H₀: no difference (equality). Hₐ: the claim (≠, <, >).
  • p-value: chance of data this extreme if H₀ were true. p ≤ α → reject H₀.
  • Fail to reject is not acceptance.
  • One-tailed vs two-tailed; independent vs paired.
  • A CI that excludes the hypothesized value means reject.
3.3.2:
Why this matters

"Statistically significant" sounds important, but it only means "probably not random chance". It says nothing about whether the difference is big enough to matter. Teams waste money acting on trivial but "significant" differences, and miss important ones because a small sample was "not significant".

The big idea

Two different questions:

  • Statistical significance: is the difference real (unlikely to be chance)? Answered by the p-value.
  • Practical significance: is the difference big enough to matter to the customer or the business? Answered by judgment, cost and specifications.

A result can be any combination of the two.

Huge samples find trivial differences

With a very large sample, even a tiny difference becomes statistically significant, because the standard error becomes tiny.

Example: two trailer-loading methods are compared on 50,000 loads. Method B is faster by 0.2 seconds, p = 0.001. Statistically significant? Yes. Practically significant? No: 0.2 seconds per load is worthless, and switching methods costs money.

Small samples miss real differences

With a small sample, even a large, important difference may not reach significance, because the test has low power (3.3.3).

Example: a pilot of a new route on 6 trips shows an average saving of 45 minutes, but p = 0.07. Concluding "the route does not help" would be wrong. The correct conclusion: insufficient evidence so far; check the power and collect more data.

Effect size and the minimum difference that matters

The effect size is how big the difference actually is (45 minutes, 0.2 seconds, 1.5 percentage points). Before testing, decide the smallest difference worth detecting (the minimum practical difference, δ). Then:

  • Size the sample so the test has enough power to detect δ (3.2.2).
  • After testing, look at the confidence interval for the difference: does it include values that matter?

Putting it together

Statistically significant?Practically significant?Action
YesYesAct on it
YesNoReal but too small to matter; usually do not act
No(large observed effect)Insufficient evidence; check power, gather more data
NoNoNo evidence of a meaningful difference

Worked example

A change reduces average tire wear by 0.01 mm per 10,000 miles, p = 0.001, with a tolerance of several millimeters. Statistically significant, not practically significant. Not worth the cost of changing.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Significant does not mean important.
  • Not significant does not mean no effect, especially with small samples.
  • Decide the practically important difference before testing.
  • Look at the size of the difference (and its CI), not just the p-value.

Check yourself

  1. Define practical significance.
  2. A study of 100,000 shipments finds a 0.05% difference in on-time rate between two systems, p < 0.001. What should you conclude?
  3. A small pilot shows a large improvement with p = 0.09. What is the right conclusion?
  4. Why should the minimum difference worth detecting be set before collecting data?
  5. What makes trivial differences "significant" in large samples?
Show answers
  1. Whether a difference is large enough to matter to the customer or the business.
  2. The difference is real (statistically significant) but too small to matter (not practically significant).
  3. Insufficient evidence; the test may lack power. Check the sample size and collect more data before deciding.
  4. So the sample can be sized to have enough power to detect it, and so the decision is not biased by the results.
  5. Very small standard errors: with huge n, almost any difference is detectable.

Key takeaways

  • Statistical significance = probably real; practical significance = big enough to matter.
  • Huge samples make trivial differences significant; small samples miss real ones.
  • Define the minimum important difference first; size the sample for it.
  • Report the effect size and confidence interval, not only the p-value.
3.3.3:
Why this matters

Every decision from a sample can be wrong in two ways: you can see a difference that is not really there, or miss one that is. Understanding these two risks lets you set them sensibly and design tests that are worth running.

The big idea

There are four possible outcomes of a test:

H₀ is actually true (no difference)H₀ is actually false (real difference)
Reject H₀Type I error (α): false alarmCorrect: real difference found (power)
Fail to reject H₀CorrectType II error (β): missed real difference

Type I error (α)

  • Rejecting H₀ when it is actually true: concluding there is a difference or effect when there is not.
  • A false alarm, a false positive.
  • Its probability is α, the significance level you choose (usually 0.05).
  • In acceptance-sampling language it is the producer's risk: rejecting a good lot, which hurts the producer.

Example: concluding the new dispatch method is faster when it really is not. You switch, spend money, and get nothing.

Type II error (β)

  • Failing to reject H₀ when it is actually false: missing a real difference.
  • A missed detection, a false negative.
  • Its probability is β.
  • In acceptance-sampling language, the consumer's risk: accepting a bad lot, which hurts the consumer.

Example: concluding the new method is no better when it really is. You miss a real improvement.

Power

Power = 1 − β

Power is the probability of detecting a real difference when one exists. A common target is 0.80 to 0.90 (80% to 90% chance of detecting the difference you care about).

Confidence level = 1 − α (95% when α = 0.05) is the probability of correctly not rejecting a true H₀.

Moving the decision line trades one risk for the other. Only a larger sample (narrower curves) or a bigger true difference reduces both.

What raises power (lowers β)

  1. Larger sample size: narrower sampling distributions, less overlap. The most common lever.
  2. Larger true difference (effect size): bigger differences are easier to see.
  3. Larger α: accepting more false-alarm risk makes it easier to reject, so fewer misses (a trade-off).
  4. Less variation (smaller σ): through better measurement or more consistent conditions.

With the sample size fixed, lowering α (being stricter about false alarms) raises β. You can only reduce both at once with more data or less noise.

Choosing α and β

  • When a false alarm is very costly (an expensive change, a safety claim), use a smaller α (0.01).
  • When missing a real effect is very costly (a safety problem goes undetected), demand higher power (0.90 or more), which needs a larger sample.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Type I = reject a true H₀ = false alarm = α = producer's risk.
  • Type II = fail to reject a false H₀ = missed detection = β = consumer's risk.
  • "Concluding the new process is better when it is not" = Type I.
  • Power = 1 − β, not 1 − α.
  • Bigger samples increase power.

Check yourself

  1. A test concludes that a new supplier's parts fail less often, but they really do not. Which error?
  2. A test fails to detect that a machine has drifted out of adjustment. Which error?
  3. β = 0.15. What is the power?
  4. Name three ways to increase power.
  5. If you lower α from 0.05 to 0.01 without changing the sample, what happens to β?
Show answers
  1. Type I (false alarm).
  2. Type II (missed detection).
  3. 0.85.
  4. Any three of: larger sample, larger effect size, larger α, smaller variation.
  5. β increases (power decreases).

Key takeaways

  • Type I (α): rejecting a true H₀, false alarm, producer's risk. Usually α = 0.05.
  • Type II (β): failing to reject a false H₀, missed detection, consumer's risk.
  • Power = 1 − β; aim for 0.80 to 0.90.
  • Power rises with larger n, larger effect, larger α, lower variation.
3.3.4:
Why this matters

"Which test should I use?" is one of the most common exam questions and one of the most important practical skills. The choice follows a small number of questions about your data and your goal. Learn the logic and the table, and the question becomes routine.

The big idea

Choose the test by asking, in this order:

  1. What type of data is the Y? Continuous or discrete (attribute)?
  2. How many groups (samples) are you comparing? One (against a target), two, or three or more?
  3. Are the groups independent, paired, or blocked?
  4. What are you comparing? Means (or medians), variances, or proportions?
  5. Is the continuous data normal? If not, use a non-parametric test (or a transformation, or rely on robustness with large samples).

The test selection table

Continuous Y, comparing centers (means or medians):

GroupsNormal data (parametric, compares means)Non-normal data (non-parametric, compares medians)
1 sample vs a target1-sample t (or Z if σ known)1-sample sign or 1-sample Wilcoxon
2 independent samples2-sample tMann-Whitney
2 paired samplesPaired tSign or Wilcoxon on the differences
3 or more independentOne-way ANOVAKruskal-Wallis, or Mood's median (if outliers)
3 or more with blocksTwo-way ANOVA (blocked)Friedman

Continuous Y, comparing spread (variances):

GroupsNormalNon-normal
1 sample vs a target1-sample variance (chi-square)(requires normality; use with care)
2 samplesF-testLevene's test
3 or moreBartlett's testLevene's test

Discrete Y (counts, proportions, categories):

SituationTest
1 proportion vs a target1-proportion test
2 proportions2-proportion test
Two categorical variables (a table of counts)Chi-square test of independence (contingency table)

Continuous Y and continuous X: correlation and regression (4.1).

Parametric vs non-parametric

  • Parametric tests (t, ANOVA, F) assume the data follow a particular distribution, usually normal, and compare means or variances.
  • Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Mood's median, sign, Wilcoxon, Friedman) make fewer assumptions. They usually work with ranks or with counts above and below the median, and compare medians (or overall distributions).
  • When the data really are normal, non-parametric tests have less power (need more data to detect the same difference). When data are clearly non-normal, especially with small samples or outliers, they are safer.

With large samples, t-tests and ANOVA are fairly robust to non-normality (thanks to the central limit theorem, 3.2.3). But for exam purposes, follow the simple fork: normal → parametric, non-normal → non-parametric.

Worked examples

  1. "Has the average delivery time of 26 hours changed? Data are normal." 1-sample t.
  2. "Compare cycle times of two shifts; data are badly skewed and samples are small." Mann-Whitney.
  3. "Compare mean fuel economy of three truck models; data normal." One-way ANOVA.
  4. "Same 12 drivers tested before and after training; normal differences." Paired t.
  5. "Did the new method reduce variation in fill weight?" Variance test: F-test if normal, Levene's if not.
  6. "Is the late-delivery rate different between two carriers?" 2-proportion test.
  7. "Is defect type related to shift?" (counts by type and shift) Chi-square contingency.
  8. "Three suppliers' lead times, skewed, with some outliers." Mood's median (or Kruskal-Wallis).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Same units before and after = paired, not 2-sample.
  • Three or more groups = ANOVA (or Kruskal-Wallis), not several t-tests.
  • "Did variation change?" = variance test, not a mean test.
  • Proportions and counts = proportion tests or chi-square, not t-tests.
  • Non-normal 2 groups = Mann-Whitney; non-normal 3+ = Kruskal-Wallis or Mood's.

Check yourself

  1. Which test compares the medians of two independent, non-normal samples?
  2. Which test checks whether the proportion of damaged loads differs between two terminals?
  3. Five suppliers' normal data on part strength: which test for means?
  4. Is a contingency table chi-square used for continuous or categorical data?
  5. A team wants to know if a new procedure reduced variation. Data are not normal. Which test?
Show answers
  1. Mann-Whitney.
  2. 2-proportion test.
  3. One-way ANOVA.
  4. Categorical (counts in categories).
  5. Levene's test.

Key takeaways

  • Decide by: data type, number of groups, independent/paired/blocked, parameter (mean, variance, proportion), normality.
  • Normal means: 1-sample t, 2-sample t, paired t, ANOVA. Non-normal: sign/Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Mood's, Friedman.
  • Variances: chi-square (1), F (2), Bartlett (3+, normal), Levene (non-normal).
  • Discrete: 1- and 2-proportion tests, chi-square contingency.
  • Non-parametric tests need fewer assumptions but have less power when data are normal.
